In today’s educational paradigm, automated question generation plays a pivotal role as it hel ps in scalable 
material production, continuous testing, and personalized learning. However, the task of generating 
academically relevant questions, which are also categorized according to the diff erent levels of cognitive 
Bloom’s taxonomy, remains a challenge. Although state-of-the-art LLM-based approa ches have improved 
the quality of questions for examination purposes, they are also marred by problems such as hallucinations, 
lack of subject matter knowledge, and lack of syllabus relevance. In contrast, con ventional rule-based and 
template-based approaches are limited to lower-order cognitive tasks. To address these issues, this paper 
proposes a Delimiting LLM framework with the concept of Retrieval-Augmented generation (RAG) for 
syllabus-relevant question generation, which is also in accordance with the differ ent levels of cognitive 
Bloom’s Taxonomy. The proposed approach can generate a variety of novel question formats by  utilizing 
RAG-based examples as few-shot learning, semantic reference context, an d exact textbook content as 
contextual grounding. The proposed approach was validated through automated and human evaluations to 
measure the quality of questions, cognitive relevance, and pedagogical si gnificance. Based on the 
experimental findings, the proposed framework outperformed conventional and non-retrieval-based 
baselines in generating cognitively diverse, syllabus-relevant, and pedagogi cally significant questions. 
Additionally, it also offers a scalable solution for smart assessment question generation. 
Keywords: Question Generation, Bloom Taxonomy, NLP, Large Language Model, Retrieval

Exams are the primary method to assess the academic value of students, which are an essential  instructional technique for improving critical thinking, active learning, and comprehension in  educational settings [1], [2], [3]. Exams are one of the most popular ways to evaluate students'  knowledge, and they call for well-written question papers. However, it takes a lot of effort and  repetition for teachers to create these questions by hand. Teachers often spend a lot of time creating  question papers because there are so many exams in the academic field, and every exam requires a  different set of questions. Automating this procedure using a machine-based  approach could assist save significant time, which can then be focused towards more beneficial  instructional initiatives. However, machine-generated questions cannot be used blindly. Automation  can speed up the process, but it does not ensure quality or exam-specific appropriateness, and many   may be unclear, inaccurate, or irrelevant. Advanced techniques like large language models (LLMs)  can assist in question generation[7], [8], but they are often fail to produce questions that correspond  with human framing styles —especially when not fine-tuned for a given educational subject and  syllabus.

A well-known system for categorizing concerns based on their level of difficulty and cognitive  complexity is Bloom's Taxonomy [9], [10]. Certain question formats can be matched to particular  Bloom's Taxonomy levels based on earlier research on question kinds and their corresponding  difficulty levels. Table 1 illustrates this mapping, which is developed from an exhaustive study of  current material as well as survey responses collected from college-level students. Fig. 2. Literature Search: a pictorial representation of the procedure      The aptness scores of six distinct question types —True/False (T/F) [3], Fill-in-the-Blank (FIB)  [11], Higher-level Fill-in-the-Blank (FIB-H), Multiple Choice Questions (MCQ) [12], Multiple- Select Questions (MSQ), and Descriptive questions—are mapped across the six Bloom's Taxonomy  cognitive levels (L1 to L6) in the diagram. The aptness score reflects how suited or aligned each  question type is for assessing the corresponding cognitive level. Nevertheless it's not the best idea to strictly link a specific question type to a set Bloom's Taxonomy  level. Large language model (LLM) technologies have made it possible to design a single question  type spanning several Blooms’ Taxonomy cognitive tiers. Therefore, the main goal of this study is  to show how even basic questions may be constructed inside an exam-specific framework to target  various Bloom's Taxonomy levels. Using LLM to generate questions is similar to a collaborative method between humans and  computers, which is crucial —using the human for exam-specific guidance and the machine for  speed. In the proposed method, the machine system is replaced with a Large Language Model  (LLM), while the human role is simulated using the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)  approach. This combination permits more effective prompt design, generating automatically  generated questions that closely mirror those crafted by people using an exam-specific manner.

In particular, we address the following three research  studies:     1. How can a Large Language Model (LLM) be effectively limited to generate questions across  different levels of Bloom’s Taxonomy for practical use inside a certain examination framework?   2. To what extent does the integration of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) technique,  paired with few-shot learning instances, effect the performance of an LLM during prompt-based  question generation?   3. To what extent does a reference-based learning approach enhance the exam alignment, structural  coherence, and quality of LLM-generated questions? The LLM generates questions aligned with Bloom's taxonomy levels based on the input context. The challenge includes instructions such as: 'You are a college teacher writing examination  questions—generate academically relevant questions from the given context.' We are able to assess  the model's highest standalone capacity because these instructions direct the LLM in question  generation without depending on any outside sources. Additionally, exam-specific sample  questions, extracted via RAG (dynamic few-shot learning from a curated dataset), are supplied  alongside user inputs. This helps the LLM produce questions that follow the style and structure of  exam-specific RAG examples [13], [14]. Once the LLM creates the questions, each one is evaluated      to determine its cognitive level within Bloom’s taxonomy, helping to assess the appropriateness of  the question type for each level.

In the proposed method, our contributions are,  RAG File Construction: The T5 model is used to generate an exam-specific RAG file that includes  questions from prior years' exams, contextual information, question types, and matching Bloom's  Taxonomy levels. In the RAG framework, this file serves as the foundation for creating dynamic  few-shot learning instances. Context-Aware Retrieval Using ANN: The RAG pipeline uses an  Artificial Neural Network (ANN)-based retrieval mechanism to find and extract contextually  aligned content in order to improve the relevance of recovered information. Reference-Based Learning Strategy: To enhance semantic grounding and the general caliber of  LLM-generated questions, other reference texts, such as preceding and succeeding contextual  sections are integrated into rapid formulation in addition to the primary context. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Part 2 discusses the relevant literature, and Part 3 of  our discussion covers our suggested approach for exam-specific question generation. Part 4 presents  the outcome of our suggested approach and a discussion of its benefits and drawbacks. In Part 5, we  finally bring our paper to a close by discussing our future plans to expand on it.

Automatic question generation (AQG) began with rule-based approaches [15], [16], particularly  geared at speeding up question paper creation in the education sector. These approaches depended  largely on predetermined rules, allowing minimal flexibility in format modifications and lacked  exam-specific adaptation. With the advent of NLP, AQG added capabilities such as generating  questions based on key phrases and part-of-speech (POS) patterns from the provided context[5],  [17]. Nevertheless, this method frequently generated semantically redundant questions, had limited  practical usefulness, and required manual feature selection. By utilizing massive datasets, deep  learning models —in particular, T5-based architectures —addressed some of these issues [18]. However, the dataset had significant effects on the generated questions' quality, and biased or  irrelevant data frequently produced useless results. Large Language Models (LLMs) represents a major advancement, using decoder-based  architectures trained on enormous corpora to generate high-quality queries [8], [19], [20]. LLM- based AQG eliminates the requirement for manual feature selection or dedicated datasets and may  create questions of any type at multiple cognitive levels. However, these algorithms are unable to  consistently generate fully aligned questions because there are no datasets particularly developed  for generating questions across various Bloom's taxonomy levels in academic settings [21], [22]. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which improves LLM performance by providing pertinent  context and sample formats, can get around this limitation [23]. RAG uses dynamic few-shot  learning [24] to give pattern-like datasets that help the model learn on its own and create exam- specific, cognitively aligned questions [25]. The RAG database is populated exclusively with computer science –related text samples to ensure  the generation of high-quality example questions.

The RAG database is populated exclusively with computer science –related text samples to ensure  the generation of high-quality example questions. By using an exam-specific RAG file, the system  provides only relevant sample questions as the reference set. These, combined with user input, are  used to produce more accurate and context-appropriate results.

The proposed method includes three core components:      1. LLM Pre-Processing: Creating a RAG-based vector database.  2. LLM Processing: Utilizing exam-specific few-shot learning through RAG.  3. LLM Post-Processing: Validating and refining the generated questions for quality and  alignment with Bloom’s Taxonomy. In the proposed approach, the user provides three inputs: the context (used as the basis for question  generation), the question type (defining the format of the question), and the cognitive level based on  Bloom’s Taxonomy (indicated as A, B, and C in the diagram) and the workflow of the proposed  method is depicted in Figure 1. These inputs are used to build a prompt, coupled with additional  reference context and some examples (D) collected via the RAG-based technique. The RAG system  offers dynamic few-shot learning by exploiting an exam-specific dataset optimized for genera ting  questions aligned with current trends. An exam-specific dataset is built using syllabus-aligned textbooks, documents, and notes, which are  scraped and pre-processed into individual sentences based on related keywords. These sentence – keyword pairs are subsequently fed into a T5 model [26], fine-tuned on the SQuAD dataset, to  generate contextually relevant questions. Fig. 1.Question Generation: Proposed method flow graph representation        As seen in Table 4, the RAG-based input process starts with a file containing four columns: context,  question type, Bloom's level, and the related generated questions. The BGE embedding technique,  which is recommended for its strong semantic similarity capabilities, effective retrieval  performance, high performance in the MTED (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark), and capacity  to lessen hallucinations in large language model (LLM) outputs, is used to embed the context  column.

Once the embedding is accomplished, the other columns —question type, Bloom’s taxonomy level,  keywords, and generated question—are paired with their relevant context embedding to form chunk  values. After that, vector representations are created from these chunk values. Lastly, the Pinecone  approach is used to index and store the vectors in a vector database. With Pinecone, the most relevant chunks are retrieved quickly, thanks to its support for ANN-based  search and hybrid search methods. Using Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) search alongside with cosine similarity, the user- provided context is first converted into an embedding, which is subsequently compared with the  pre-stored embedding in the vector database of the RAG file. This similarity-based retrieval delivers  the most relevant text chunks from the Pinecone vector database. To enhance the precision of  retrieval, further filtering can be done using metadata values —such as selecting Bloom Level =  Apply and Question Type = MCQ—in conjunction with the user's inputs. This combined method of  semantic similarity search and metadata-based filtering ensures more accurate and contextually  relevant results from the vector database. The LLM is prompted to create new, contextually relevant questions using the obtained data (row- based). The LLM models, which are well-suited for RAG-based systems because of their powerful  few-shot learning capabilities, receive these chunks as input and use them as dynamic few-shot  learning examples. The RAG-retrieved sample content and user inputs are used by the LLM to  produce questions. After the question is created, it is filtered and assessed according to its relevance  score.

The ranges of sample question decided by the  situation and needs. The second aspect is that question papers should be aligned with patterns observed in previous  years to avoid ambiguity for students. While the questions need not be identical, those with similar  structural formats should be treated equivalently. To achieve this, the proposed method employs a  Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, where previous years’ questions serve as  reference material for generating new questions across different Bloom’s taxonomy levels and  multiple question types. In general, the results clearly show that there is a synergistic effect between RAG and RCL in  improving the performance of the LLM, and that the combination of the two yields the best results. The model that performs best in all experimental conditions is Mistral, which adapts and improves  exceptionally well when prompted with both RAG and RCL. These results clearly indicate that  hybrid approaches to prompting are necessary for maximizing the interpretability, correctness, and   usefulness of the generated responses, especially in complex tasks that require a lot of information. When the LLM is used alone, the question that is generated is very similar to the source sentence,  which results in a direct recall-based item with very little linguistic variation. The use of example   formats to guide the LLM is improved by Reference-based Learning Constraints (RLC), which  improve the quality of the questions by allowing for more varied and pedagogically formatted  questions without deviating from the desired cognitive level.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is another improvement that provides more contextual  grounding, which allows the model to generate questions that are both semantically accurate and  faithful to the original content. Overall, the combined LLM + RLC + RAG framework achieves superior balance among accuracy,  diversity, and educational relevance , making it well-suited for automated question generation in  academic assessment systems[27]. As presented in Table 4, while the differences between various LLM models are not statistically 
significant, the employment of Reference Context Learning (RCL) and Retrieval-Augmented 
Generation (RAG) produces substantial performance enhancements. The study finds that the 
synergistic application of RCL and RAG leads to superior results compared to either technique used 
in isolation, establishing the combined approach as the most effective.

Table 5 presents a comparative assessment of the question generation capability of three large  language model platforms, namely OpenAI, Ollama, and Gemini, for three different experimental  setups: baseline LLM, Reference Context Learning (RCL), and Retrieval-Augmented generation  (RAG). The automatic evaluation criteria, such as BLEU [28], ROUGE (ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2,  ROUGE-3) [29], METEOR [30], and F1 score, are used to assess the performance of the models. These criteria collectively assess the lexical overlap, semantic similarity, and content coverage of  the generated questions and the reference questions. The automatic evaluation criteria clearly indicate the improvement trajectory of the OpenAI model. The baseline setup showed very low scores for BLEU (0.015) and ROUGE, which clearly indicated  the lack of n-gram overlap between the generated questions and the reference questions. However,  the RCL setup showed a significant improvement in the scores, with ROUGE-1 and METEOR  scores increasing to 0.327 and 0.257, respectively. The best performance was achieved by the RAG  setup, which showed the highest scores for ROUGE-2 (0.318), ROUGE-3 (0.286), and F1 (0.432). This demonstrates that retrieving and incorporating external knowledge is most effective for  improving contextual relevance and lexical coverage. A similar pattern can be observed in the Ollama-based model. The baseline LLM arrangement  performs mediocrely, especially in ROUGE-1 (0.222) and BLEU (0.003). Significant improvements  are gained with the Reference Context Learning approach, particularly in METEOR (0.327) and F1  score (0.419), which suggest enhanced semantic alignment. Competitive ROUGE-2 (0.279) and  ROUGE-3 (0.244) scores are produced by the RAG design, demonstrating the effectiveness of  retrieval processes in increasing phrase-level similarity and overall completeness.

With ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-3 scores of zero, the baseline LLM results for the Gemini-based  model are rather poor and show little higher-order n-gram overlap. However, the RAG-based  technique produces additional improvements in ROUGE-2 (0.238) and ROUGE-3 (0.200), while  the Reference Context Learning setting raises ROUGE-1 to 0.291 and F1 to 0.318. The findings show that RAG regularly outperforms baseline LLM and RCL configurations on every 
platform. ROUGE and F1 measures, which more accurately reflect the semantic relevance and 
quality necessary for question production, are where this superiority is most obvious. While 
Reference Context Learning (RCL) provides a valuable step up from zero-shot prompting, it 
remains an intermediate solution. Notably, the models' low BLEU scores indicate that BLEU is not 
a good fit for tasks requiring lexical diversity; on the other hand, ROUGE, METEOR, and F1 
provide a more accurate assessment of content coverage.

Qualitative results in Table 5 above further confirm these results. Although the baseline and RCL 
settings of OpenAI resulted in the same average score of 3.17, the RAG-based approach resulted in 
 
 
a better score of 4.33. Most importantly, RAG received a perfect score of 5 on relevance, 
emphasizing its capability to make use of external context information for generating high-quality 
and specific questions. Analysis of Ollama and Gemini-based models shows that the Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) approach is the best-performing configuration, as it results in the 
highest final scores and performs best on relevance, answerability, and specificity.  
Among the models, Ollama showed the greatest improvement with RAG, as its score improved 
from 3.50 to 4.50. Although the Reference Context Learning (RCL) approach showed moderate 
improvement in clarity and usability, its effect was always overshadowed by that of RAG. The 
overall results clearly show a performance hierarchy: Baseline < RCL < RAG < RAG + R CL. This 
result clearly shows that the best possible approach is to combine the capability of external 
knowledge retrieval (RAG) with example-based prompting (RCL). Moreover, this study confirms 
that human-centric evaluation criteria are necessary for measuring these subtle qualitative 
improvements. 
 
 
Fig. 3. Performance Comparison: Question generation with various approaches

The questions that are specific to exams and based on the syllabus cannot be generated by 
enhancing the overall capability of the LLM. Rather, by keeping the LLM within certain 
constraints, better results can be achieved, which will allow the LLM to generate questions in a 
more focused way. The fact that the technique performs well on all types of questions and levels of 
Bloom's taxonomy indicates that an LLM with a linear bound can perform very well if it is given 
the right input, such as proper prompts, few-shot examples, and reference questions using RAG. 
This technique can be improved in the future to generate mathematical and programming-related 
questions, along with text questions.
